title: Proofs with Quantifiers
short: Strip the quantifiers (EI before UI), reason with the propositional rules, then put quantifiers back with UG or EG.
trouble: Learners use UI first and then cannot use EI with a new name. Do EI first when both are needed.

blocks.html: You now have all four quantifier rules (UI, EG, EI, UG) and quantifier negation (QN). This lesson puts them together into a strategy for predicate proofs, building on Universal Generalization (UG).
Strip the quantifiers (use QN first if a premise starts with a negation; then EI before UI), reason with the propositional rules, then put quantifiers back with EG or UG as the conclusion requires.

Once the quantifiers are off, the lines are just like statement logic: $Fa \to Ga$ behaves like $p \to q$. So all the proof skills of the earlier units carry over. The quantifier rules are the doors in and out. Their restrictions decide the order: EI needs a fresh name, so it goes first; UG needs an arbitrary variable, so plan for it from the start.

Plan
rows: UI with that name; propositional rules
get an instance with some name, then EG
UI with a variable, then UG at the end
aim for the QN form, then QN

lines.note: EI first, with a new name.

blocks.title: Start with QN
blocks.q: Premises $\forall x(Fx \to Gx)$ and $\neg \forall x Gx$. Prove $\exists x\neg Fx$.

blocks.title: A universal conclusion
blocks.q: Premises $\forall x Fx$ and $\forall x Gx$. Prove $\forall x(Fx \land Gx)$.
steps: Line 3: $Fy$ by UI 1. Line 4: $Gy$ by UI 2.

blocks.html: Using UI first and then being unable to use EI with a new name. In the example above, if line 3 had been $Fa \to Ga$ by UI, then $\exists x Gx$ could no longer be instantiated to $a$, and the proof would stall. Do EI first when both are needed.

Why does the second example use variables instead of names? Because the conclusion is universal and must end with UG, which only works on a variable. Had line 3 been $Fa$, the proof would reach $Fa \land Ga$ and then be stuck, since UG never applies to a name.

If a proof seems impossible, it may be invalid. Before searching too long, try to build a counterexample world: if you find one, no proof exists. If every attempt at a world fails, that is a good sign a proof is there to be found.

items: Negated quantifier in a premise? QN.
Existential premises: EI, each with its own new name.
Universal premises: UI, with those names (or a variable if the conclusion is universal).
